article_text:
渋谷のアートブック書店、東塔堂にて原田直宏の写真展「2」が開催される。

本展では、2009年から2011年にかけて撮影された東京の道行く人々を撮影した作品「Drifting」と、2018年から2021年にかけて、東京の道で魚をファッションモデルのように撮影した「Tokyo Fishgraphs」の２つのシリーズの作品を展開。どちらも前作のセレクションで選ばれなかった未公開写真の中から、新たに選ばれた写真を中心に展示が構成されている。

写真展の「2」というタイトルには、続編の意味が込められており、初作と続編の関係性、時間を経て選び直されたイメージ等、普段取り上げられることの少ないアートブックの続編が出来上がる経緯や意味を考察できる内容となっている。2つの旧作の未公開写真を通して、アートにおける「続編」とは何かを考える機会となるだろう。

会期中にはアーティストトークも予定されており、これまでのアーティスト活動、制作のきっかけ、海外出版社との仕事等について語られる。

article_text:
The edict at Netflix has always been, we want you to watch movies on Netflix. It has begrudgingly put some movies into theaters for awards-qualifying runs or to appease auteur filmmakers like Guillermo del Toro and Martin Scorsese, and it has even purchased and restored a few movie palaces to demonstrate its love of cinema.

But putting movies into theaters and boasting about how much money they make has never been its M.O. Even when it looks like it has a hit on its hands with a sing-a-long version of “KPop Demon Hunters,” Netflix has never wanted to take a victory lap, because doing so would open it up to having egg on its face when things don’t go so well. Hits and flops come for every studio. Just ask Apple how it enjoyed the scrutiny it received back when it was all in on theatrical.

That’s finally changing with Netflix’s big awards play of 2026, Cannes and TIFF darling “La Bola Negra.” It’s an ambitious and sweeping Spanish war and LGBTQ epic that demands to be seen on the big screen because of how it has inspired record-breaking standing ovations and won audience awards from the festival crowds who have seen it. The film will open in limited release on just four screens on Friday in both Los Angeles and New York, including at Netflix’s The Paris and also two major AMCs in Los Angeles, a chain that historically refused to play Netflix films.

Co-CEO Ted Sarandos in his Screentime conference interview said that Netflix released 30 movies into theaters last year, each with their own bespoke, limited release strategy, and that “ La Bola Negra ” is really no different.

What is different is that it will offer the longest theatrical exclusive window — 47 days — it has ever offered before the film drops on streaming, and it will be the first time it’s actually reporting what the movie makes in theaters. The hope is that a strong per-screen-average will lead to a longer word-of-mouth campaign for the film over those 47 days, and it is designing the platform rollout in a way that it won’t harm the movie once it goes on streaming later.

“We’re looking at this model and saying, how do we serve movie lovers who may want to see this movie in a theater, and how do we not harm value to Netflix, and how do we position the film best in the world,” Sarandos said. He added that it requires treating art house films like “La Bola Negra” and “Train Dreams” differently than how it treats four-quadrant films like Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” or its animated “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” film.

Whatever “La Bola Negra” makes, it will be a box office record for Netflix, but only because Netflix has literally not publicly reported what any of its other theatrical, awards plays have brought in over the years. Not once. The streamer has bucked a tradition that every film studio has always done when discussing the performance of their films, and it has created the perception that, fair or not, Netflix hasn’t cared about theaters and the theatrical experience the way others have.

Netflix’s messaging began changing when it was lined up to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s film assets, before Paramount swooped in with a better deal for the whole entity. Suddenly CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters were talking about how much they loved movie theaters , and they were throwing around promises about 45-day windows to convince skeptics about how it would be handling a legacy studio like Warner Bros.

So why is Netflix doing all this now, and why with a movie like “La Bola Negra,” which doesn’t have stars, isn’t in English, and isn’t based on IP? Because Sarandos is a smart cookie. Perhaps contrary to some belief, Sarandos didn’t crack open Warner Bros.’ books and realize for the first time that movies can actually make money in theaters.

Coming up later this year is another potential awards play with David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” which is a sequel to a box office hit and stars Brad Pitt. It also just dropped the first trailer for its highly-anticipated “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” from Gerwig coming early next year, and it wouldn’t be a surprise if people saw that trailer playing ahead of “La Bola Negra” screenings. Both of those films, as well as Danny Boyle’s “Ink” and Peter Berg’s “Mosquito Bowl,” will have traditional box office reporting just as “La Bola Negra” does.

With “Cliff Booth” and “Narnia,” those films are each in IMAX, and Netflix is currently having conversations with exhibitors on “Cliff Booth” to lock in that film’s footprint, but AMC and its roughly 200-300 IMAX locations have already agreed to screen it over Thanksgiving. “Narnia” will open even wider beyond just IMAX , and the hope is that both of these major tentpoles can deliver strong results.

“La Bola Negra” then is the test balloon of sorts, even if it ends up not being a major hit. It will let Netflix get its feet wet for how it will report data moving forward and how it can hone that process before “Cliff Booth” and “Narnia.” That’s important because what Netflix has not done as it has ramped up its theatrical ambitions is aggressively hire numerous executives who are experienced in the theatrical space. Netflix’s distribution chief, Spencer Klein, has been with Netflix for some time and knows the nuts and bolts of reporting box office from his stints at Fox and The Weinstein Company, and its existing team has had experience with these platform releases over the years. That’s not a worry. But it hasn’t sought out new talent to determine how to best market and release these films in a theatrical-first setting. And it ultimately did not buy a movie studio that has all of those people and processes built in. Netflix did recently enlist Katie Martin Kelly , a veteran of Warner Bros. and Paramount, to join its communications team.

But to secure these relationships with exhibitors and get the screens it needs to make theatrical viable, IndieWire understands Netflix has had to agree to some more favorable terms than those that theaters usually reserve for other major studios, which tends to be an even 50-50 split of ticket sales. That might’ve also been necessary as a means of getting a theatrically exclusive window that Netflix wants. Netflix had no comment to add.

There’s a few things that may have changed that led Netflix to this point, and the streamer’s rationale is likely a combination of all of them rather than just one. The first, most obvious one is that theatrical brings in a caliber of filmmaker that Netflix has had trouble securing previously , with Gerwig on the top of that list. Star talent also needs box office, not just streaming figures, to secure those bigger paydays down the road. The second is that Netflix likely has seen how its licensing deal with Sony has worked for those films: generally, the Sony movies that perform best in theaters are the ones that also perform best on Netflix (with some exceptions for something like “Madame Web” ), though Sarandos argued in his Screentime interview that theatrical films don’t necessarily outperform all of Netflix’s other originals. Third, if Netflix wants to be able to release movies in theaters and then quickly move them directly to Netflix, the window to do so may be closing as other studios start to agree to other windowing standards about when a movie can go from theaters to PVOD and then to SVOD.

But the real challenge that may be tipping the scales is that any streamer, not just Netflix, is starting to hit a plateau of finding new subscribers in the U.S. market ( Netflix no longer regularly reports its total subscribers either , saying revenue is its main metric of success). Netflix has introduced an ad-supported pricing tier, it has gone heavy on live events and sports, it has ramped up gaming and podcasts. It has to find something else different in order to help its bread and butter of growing the streaming service. Putting movies in theaters and reaching a crowd that perhaps doesn’t normally subscribe to streaming but might be convinced if they know this big movie it has made will eventually be there, could be a smart approach toward growth. Netflix just on Wednesday laid off about 1,000 workers , one of its biggest staffing cuts in its history, because of that slower growth.

The extra piece Netflix has to contend with is marketing spending. Theatrical movies require shelling out tens of millions of dollars on trailers and promotional materials to create awareness and get people out to the theater, which is a bigger ask than getting them to click a button to start streaming a movie they may not have heard of. Many studios have a habit of throwing a lot of good money after bad in hawking a movie, even when a film is underperforming ( here’s looking at you “Digger” ), so finding the right balance is something Netflix will have to figure out.

But the secret that streamers like Amazon and Apple ( when it was tinkering with theatrical ) have figured out is that, though they want all these movies to be theatrical hits, if the box office can cover the marketing costs, it’s done its job and essentially provided a big free marketing campaign for when the movie is set to hit streaming. It’s been proven that movies that have that theatrical push tend to perform better on streaming down the road, and Netflix may finally want to reap the benefits of that. Sarandos said if a movie is going to take somewhat of a hit on Netflix itself by going theatrical, it should be because it has big upside at the box office. Moreover, how many Netflix original movies have entered the cultural conversation the way theatrical films have? “KPop Demon Hunters,” “The Kissing Booth,” maybe “Bird Box” and some others, and after that it gets challenging unless you’re a “Bright” stan.

Netflix will likely say that even with these big movies coming to theaters soon, it reporting box office numbers doesn’t represent a shift in strategy on the whole . It still produces dozens of movies that are only streaming plays and will do great with or without theatrical. But it does represent a shift for the industry on the whole. And if a few Netflix successes can create a more robust theatrical marketplace, it benefits everyone.

Tate Modern’s first ever exhibition focusing exclusively on Claude Monet brings together breathtaking paintings from lenders across the globe, including rarely seen works from private collections.

Based mainly in France, Monet lived through an era which saw the rise of railways, industrialisation, the modern city, and the adoption of standardised timekeeping. Drawing on new research, the show explores how Monet responded to these seismic changes through his work.

The exhibition centres on Monet’s profound and evolving relationship with time. We see how he echoed the rapid pace of modern life by capturing the fleeting, instantaneous ‘impressionist’ moment, through works such as Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare (1877). We are also shown, in celebrated series such as Poplars on the Epte (1891–1897), Monet’s attempts, through variations of the same subject, to capture a specific, transient instant in time.

Finally, the show reveals Monet’s enduring relationship with nature and how, as a subject in perpetual movement, it shifts with the passing years and seasons. We see his retreat into his beloved garden in Giverny, resulting in the creation of the world-famous Water Lilies cycle.

Monet: Painting Time is supported by Lead Supporter, Morgan Stanley. Further support from Anthropic. With additional support from the Monet: Painting Time Exhibition Supporters Circle, Tate Members and Tate Americas Foundation. Exhibition organised by Tate Modern and Musée de l'Orangerie.

article_text:
“ Other Mommy ” may have dominated “ The Social Reckoning ” at the box office this past weekend, but there’s no hard feelings between longtime friends Jessica Chastain and Jeremy Strong .

Chastain, who stars as a demonic mother in horror movie “Other Mommy,” shared on her Instagram Story Monday night a playful string of text messages with Strong, who plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up.

Related Stories

Strong texted Chastain a Vulture headline about “Other Mommy’s” box office success which read, “‘Other Mommy’ Spanks ‘The Social Reckoning’ at the Box Office.” Indeed, it did — “Other Mommy” scored the No. 1 spot with $27.5 million , while “The Social Reckoning” flopped with just $5.5 million.

“Omg,” Chastain replied, to which Strong fired back with a middle finger emoji and kiss emoji.

“These pics are hysterical,” Chastain commented of Vulture’s photo choice, featuring them side-by-side in character. “Its so funny,” Strong said, to which Chastain responded: “You look SO SAD!”

“Other Mommy” debuted well above box office expectations, considering the fact that it received poor reviews and a D+ grade on CinemaScore. With a budget of just $18 million, Blumhouse and Universal’s campy thriller is well positioned financially.

“The Social Reckoning,” on the other hand, failed to live up to its projected debut of $7 million to $8 million. Critics were mixed on the film, which follows a Facebook engineer (Mikey Madison) who leaks thousands of internal documents to a reporter (Jeremy Allen White) to blow the whistle on the company’s dark practices. Strong once again went Method to portray Zuckerberg, with Sorkin telling The New York Times that the actor treated his co-stars “the way he imagines” Zuckerberg would.

“I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him,'” Sorkin said. “And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.”

"蚕茧是你亲手就能触摸到的转化，这太迷人了！就像蚕一样，我认为我们人类也是以一种形态进入某种境地，出来时发生了改变。但与蚕不同的是，我们的转化不止一次。随着身体的老年化、智慧的增长以及我们重新发现自己是谁、来自何方，我们在一生中不断地进行着这种转化。这也是我希望《神圣之器》所能做到的：不仅仅是表现疗愈，而是让体验这场展览的人们经历他们自己的转化。塔萨尼·杜雷特，《精神海岸线》（Shorelines Collection）将大西洋视为一个由创伤、知识、流动和祖先记忆塑造的空间。海洋如何塑造你对‘Sacred Vessels ’中历史与经历的思考？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大西洋是承载了海量黑人历史的地方，这些历史被同时承载、中断又重写。创伤、知识、流动和祖先记忆都穿过了同一片水域。当人们想到黑人历史和海洋时，通常会停留在中大西洋航路（Middle Passage）。我从未想过忘记这一点。但“黑人海事收藏”（Black Maritime Collection）也讲述了那些被遗漏的故事：黑人水手、捕鲸者、船长、救生员以及在同一片水域上建立生活、财富和自由的捕鱼社区。威廉·T·索里（William T. Shorey）船长最初是一名船舱工人，后来成为1800年代太平洋海岸最受尊敬和知名的黑人捕鲸船长之一。他的故事与中大西洋航路（Middle Passage）属于同一片海洋。海洋曾是一个充满失落的地方，对我们许多人来说，它也是一个充满技艺、独立和自豪的地方。我想向这两者致敬。在创作‘Sacred Vessels’的同时创作“黑人海事收藏”（Black Maritime Collection），这提醒我水不仅仅会分离。它还会承载。它在距离中传递事物而没有将其完全摧毁。这也是我对自我和材料的要求。海洋教会我，记忆可以穿越破裂并依然抵达某处，将痛苦与胜利一同承载。这种双重性是这两组作品之间的贯穿线。Tasanee Durrett，‘ Oceanic Origins ‘，2025年。图片由艺术家提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Oceanic-Origins-1028x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Tasanee Durrett，‘ Oceanic Origins ‘，2025年。图片由艺术家提供。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的作品是通过将材料层层叠加和嵌入绘画表面来构建的。这种构筑在每件作品的意义中扮演什么角色？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一名建筑师，我协调并建造商业建筑，而我画画的方式也正是我对待建筑的方式。我将每一幅画都视为一个需要解决的问题。我一层一层地构建它，每个部分都必须与其他部分协同工作，就像建筑的系统汇聚成一个运作的整体一样。每一层丙烯颜料，以及我在湿画笔中压入拉菲草、蚕茧或盐的每一个地方，都是该结构的一部分。最终，这幅画就像一台讲故事的机器一样运作。我认为建筑是有生命的东西。它们讲述了身处其中之人的故事，而这些人反过来又塑造了建筑。我的画作也是如此。我在构建每件作品时都在讲述一个故事，但一旦有人站在它面前，他们就会带来自己的经历。每位观众都会抽出自己的线索，因此故事不断超越我所注入的内容而生长。Tasanee ‘，2026年。图片由艺术家提供。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当观众接触到‘Sacred Vessels ’时，关于记忆、传承和疗愈，你通过展览继续探索哪些问题？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不断回想起，要让某物得到良好的传承究竟需要什么，不仅仅是传下去，而是以一种能够被承载下去的方式被接收。我还在不断探问，当疗愈尚未解决、当伤口和修复在同一件作品中依然清晰可见时，疗愈会是什么样子。‘Sacred Vessels’与其说是在回答这些问题，不如说是在为它们留出空间，正如我希望人们也能通过作品中的视觉故事来看待彼此和其他文化一样。", "translated": true}, In her solo exhibition ‘Sacred Vessels: Healing and Memory in the Black Diaspora ‘ , the artist and architect works with acrylic, raffia, salt and silkworm cocoons to explore transformation, inheritance and repair. Moving between personal experiences of rebuilding and the wider histories of the Black diaspora, Durrett considers how memory survives rupture and how materials can carry histories of their own. In conversation with ART AFRICA , she discusses architecture as a way of thinking, the Atlantic as a site of both trauma and possibility, and what it means to make healing visible without suggesting that it is ever fully resolved. But the head is different for every one of us, whatever our background or race. It holds our identity, our memories, and everything we have lived through. The eyes matter to me too. That same logic carries into how I think about the body, as a structure with load, grain, and thresholds, not just a subject to depict. When I’m building a piece, I’m asking the same questions an architect asks about a room: what does this space need to hold, where does weight need to be carried, where is the opening? Image Courtesy of Artist.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Raffia, salt, and silkworm cocoons appear throughout your work, each carrying particular histories and associations. Raffia carries a West African textile and hair tradition in its fibre, so when I work with it I’m not inventing a meaning; I’m continuing one. I press salt into the wet paint as a reminder that we are salt people. Salt is in our blood, our sweat, and our tears, and it has its own long history in healing traditions around the world. Silkworm cocoons hold the physical proof of transformation in how something enters one state and leaves in another. None of these is symbols I chose from the outside. We do it again and again over a lifetime as our bodies age, as we grow wiser, and as we rediscover who we are and where we come from. How does the ocean shape your thinking about the histories and experiences in ‘Sacred Vessels ’ ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Atlantic is where a huge amount of Black history was carried, interrupted, and rewritten, all at once. Trauma, knowledge, movement, and ancestral memory all moved through the same water. When people think of Black history and the ocean, they usually stop at the Middle Passage. I never want to forget that. But the Black Maritime Collection also tells the stories that get left out: Black sailors, whalers, ship captains, lifesavers, and fishing communities who built lives, wealth, and freedom on that same water. Captain William T. Shorey began as a cabin worker and became one of the most respected and well-known Black whaling captains on the Pacific coast in the 1800s. His story belongs in the same ocean as the Middle Passage. The ocean was a place of loss, and for many of us it was also a place of skill, independence, and pride. I want to honour both. Working on the Black Maritime Collection alongside ‘Sacred Vessels’ reminds me that water doesn’t only separate. It also holds. It carries things across distance without destroying them completely. That’s what I ask of myself and my materials too. The ocean taught me that memory can travel through rupture and still arrive somewhere, carrying the pain and the triumph together. That duality is the throughline between the two bodies of work. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Oceanic Origins ‘, 2025. In ‘Sacred Vessels ‘ , Tasanee Durrett brings architecture, material and personal history into conversation, asking how memory is held, transformed and carried across generations.

For Tasanee Durrett, the body is both structure and vessel, a place where memory, identity and lived experience accumulate. In her solo exhibition ‘Sacred Vessels: Healing and Memory in the Black Diaspora ‘ , the artist and architect works with acrylic, raffia, salt and silkworm cocoons to explore transformation, inheritance and repair. Moving between personal experiences of rebuilding and the wider histories of the Black diaspora, Durrett considers how memory survives rupture and how materials can carry histories of their own. In conversation with ART AFRICA , she discusses architecture as a way of thinking, the Atlantic as a site of both trauma and possibility, and what it means to make healing visible without suggesting that it is ever fully resolved. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Crab Hands In Deep Waters ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Suzette Bell-Roberts: ‘Sacred Vessels’ brings together healing, memory, and the Black diaspora. Within the exhibition, what does a “vessel” mean, and how did it become the framework for these works?

Tasanee Durett: To me, a vessel is what holds our emotions, experiences, and stories. That is why, in my figurative work, I mostly paint and draw from the neck up. I see the head as the true vessel. From the neck down, our bodies are largely the same. But the head is different for every one of us, whatever our background or race. It holds our identity, our memories, and everything we have lived through. The eyes matter to me too. Biologically, they grow out of the brain itself, so I feel that when we look into someone’s eyes, we’re looking at the mind. The neck is what carries that vessel. It holds up the mind and the psyche. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Endure Endure Endure ‘, 2024. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your practice moves between architecture and painting. How has your architectural training shaped your thinking about space, structure, and the body?

Architecture taught me to think with my hands before I think in words, and that instinct never left me. My continuous, unbroken line comes directly from that training, thinking while drawing rather than drawing what I’ve already decided. That same logic carries into how I think about the body, as a structure with load, grain, and thresholds, not just a subject to depict. When I’m building a piece, I’m asking the same questions an architect asks about a room: what does this space need to hold, where does weight need to be carried, where is the opening? The body in my work functions the same way. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ I Am, We Are Agave ‘, 2024. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Raffia, salt, and silkworm cocoons appear throughout your work, each carrying particular histories and associations. How do you approach material as memory and storytelling?

I try to let the material tell me what it already knows before I ask it to say anything else. Raffia carries a West African textile and hair tradition in its fibre, so when I work with it I’m not inventing a meaning; I’m continuing one. I press salt into the wet paint as a reminder that we are salt people. Salt is in our blood, our sweat, and our tears, and it has its own long history in healing traditions around the world. Silkworm cocoons hold the physical proof of transformation in how something enters one state and leaves in another. None of these is symbols I chose from the outside. They’ve become materials with their own inherited stories and histories, and my job is to build with that history intact rather than erase it. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ The Oyster King Lives On ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Physically and conceptually, transformation appears in your materials, particularly through silkworm cocoons. In ‘Sacred Vessels’, how does transformation operate?

Silkworm cocoons are transformation you can literally hold in your hand, and it’s fascinating! Like the silkworm, I see us as human beings going into something as one form and coming out changed. But unlike the silkworm, we don’t transform just once. We do it again and again over a lifetime as our bodies age, as we grow wiser, and as we rediscover who we are and where we come from. That is what I want Sacred Vessels to do too: not solely represent healing, but allow those who experience the show to undergo their own transformation. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Shorelines of the Spirit ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Alongside questions of identity and lineage, the exhibition considers psychological healing within the Black diaspora. How do you relate personal memory to diasporic history?

My own path through rupture and rebuilding, coming out of an eight-year abusive relationship and finding my way back to myself, shows up in the work less as subject and more as method. Repair is how I make things now. When I connect that to diasporic history, I’m not claiming my story stands in for a larger one; I’m noticing that the pattern is the same and that when something is broken, knowledge or memory gets interrupted, and then, generations or years later, it resurfaces and gets rebuilt into something new. Sacred Vessels holds both scales at once, my own healing and the diaspora’s, because I don’t think they operate on different logic. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Tethered Waters ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your ongoing Black Maritime Collection engages with the Atlantic as a space shaped by trauma, knowledge, movement, and ancestral memory. How does the ocean shape your thinking about the histories and experiences in ‘Sacred Vessels ’ ?

The Atlantic is where a huge amount of Black history was carried, interrupted, and rewritten, all at once. Trauma, knowledge, movement, and ancestral memory all moved through the same water. When people think of Black history and the ocean, they usually stop at the Middle Passage. I never want to forget that. But the Black Maritime Collection also tells the stories that get left out: Black sailors, whalers, ship captains, lifesavers, and fishing communities who built lives, wealth, and freedom on that same water. Captain William T. Shorey began as a cabin worker and became one of the most respected and well-known Black whaling captains on the Pacific coast in the 1800s. His story belongs in the same ocean as the Middle Passage. The ocean was a place of loss, and for many of us it was also a place of skill, independence, and pride. I want to honour both. Working on the Black Maritime Collection alongside ‘Sacred Vessels’ reminds me that water doesn’t only separate. It also holds. It carries things across distance without destroying them completely. That’s what I ask of myself and my materials too. The ocean taught me that memory can travel through rupture and still arrive somewhere, carrying the pain and the triumph together. That duality is the throughline between the two bodies of work. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Oceanic Origins ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your works are built through layering and embedding materials into painted surfaces. What role does this construction play in meaning in each work?

As an architect, I coordinate and construct commercial buildings, and I paint the same way I approach construction. I see each painting as a problem to solve. I build it up layer by layer, and every part has to work with the others, the way a building’s systems come together into one working whole. Each coat of acrylic and each place I press raffia, cocoons, or salt into the wet paint is part of that structure. By the end, the painting works like a machine that tells a story. I see buildings as living things. They tell the stories of the people inside them, and those people shape the building in return. My paintings work the same way. I tell a story as I build each piece, but once someone stands in front of it, they bring their own experiences. Every viewer pulls out their own threads, so the story keeps growing beyond what I put into it. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Access To Water For Brown Bodies II ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

As audiences encounter ‘Sacred Vessels ’ , what questions about memory, inheritance, and healing do you continue to explore through the exhibition?

I keep coming back to what it actually takes for something to be inherited well, not just passed down but received in a way that can be carried forward. And I keep asking what healing looks like when it’s not resolved, when the wound and the repair are both still visible in the same piece. ‘Sacred Vessels’ doesn’t answer those questions so much as it holds space for them, the way I hope people also see each other, and other cultures, through the visual stories in the work.

This exhibition is on view at the Hannibal Square Heritage Center in Florida until 13 December 2026.

article_text:
Simon Reynolds’s Still in a Dream is an eloquent, enduring argument for an art of bliss and bewilderment

The subtitle of Simon Reynolds’s book spans a wide spectrum of music. Beginning with the ‘ethereal world’ of Cocteau Twins and the enigmatic murmuring of early R.E.M., the music critic goes on to exalt the cultivated miserabilism of The Smiths and Felt; the jet-stream distortion haze of Hüsker Du and Band of Susans; the hollering surrealism of Pixies and Throwing Muses; Butthole Surfers’ body-horror grotesquery; the narcotic drone of Spacemen 3; the swooning introspection of Slowdive; Big Black’s brutalising, machinic punk-metal; and even the tune-down riff-reveries of first-wave grunge. Yet uniting all this – as signalled in the title quote from My Bloody Valentine’s emblematic 1988 track (When You Wake) You’re Still in a Dream – is a thesis on withdrawal.

The historical narrative is loosely this: in the wake of fiery punk heat and colder postpunk calculation, an array of independent scenes and underground artists advanced in a spirit of creative retreat: backing away from arch or ardent lyrical content, burying vocals deep in the mix or surrendering to waves of intensely saturated guitar effects. For some, stage presence was defined by self-conscious diffidence. In songs, allusions to everyday life were abandoned in favour of dream-state abstraction or delirious, absurdist fantasy. For Reynolds, one embryonic instance of these secessionist tendencies is mid-1980s ‘anorak’ indie: acts like Talulah Gosh (featuring artist Elizabeth Price) who crafted styles of fauxnaïf teen innocence in both their anti-glamour appearance and lovelorn lo-fi guitar pop. But it’s the era’s more overwhelming sonic tides – submerging the listener in drenching sound – that Reynolds treasures as supremely galvanising aesthetic experiences. A chapter on selfdeclared ‘dreampop’ duo AR Kane paints the modest oeuvre of Alex Ayuli and Rudy Tambala as near unsurpassed in its discordant, destabilising beauty. Fusing dub reggae’s echo-spaces with rock’s electric dissonance and the improvisatory freedoms of far-out jazz, this was music as engulfing miasma – experiments in ‘guitar reinvention’ rivalled only at that time, Reynolds believes, by Sonic Youth and My Bloody Valentine.

Drawing on his time as a staff writer on Melody Maker , Reynolds remembers moments of intellectual ambition: linking the ‘dazed and defused’ feel of Sonic Youth’s Daydream Nation (1988) to Paul Auster’s 1985 novel City of Glass , for instance, or comparing the ‘melted sound’ of My Bloody Valentine (as described by frontman Kevin Shields) to lines by Roland Barthes (‘I fall, I flow, I melt’). Such recollections of youthful critical questing represent something distinctive within the continuum of Reynolds’s writings. (By my count, Still in a Dream is his tenth book.) Here, his autobiographical presence offers a counterpoint to the book’s focus on artistic self-effacement: Still in a Dream tells a story of personal discovery, revisiting situations of revelation, transformative encounters with new music, new places, new loves. And if sometimes the retrospective view allows Reynolds to raise an eyebrow at the callow convictions of his early-career criticism, mostly he remains keen to honour his onetime commitment to all-consuming rapture, paying tribute to the zealous vitality of writing that risked ‘absurdity by taking things too seriously’.

The coinage ‘shoegaze’ first surfaced as a snarky music-press riposte to Melody Maker ’s rhapsodic coverage of neo-psychedelic guitar bands. But like many former slurs, the term has shaken off its mocking associations. Though not one of Reynolds’s favoured designations, he nonetheless sees how a shoegaze ‘aestheticism of surrender’ retains its cultural worth. (‘Slacker’ rock, he argues, has similar virtues: soundtracking dejected withdrawal with swells of immersive noise.) Framed by Thatcherism in Britain and the Reagan–Bush hegemony in the US, Reynolds historicises his preferred schools of 1980s and 90s underground rock as resistant partisans of ‘desire and dream’, pitting ‘intensified existence’ against ‘the coarsening values of the mainstream’. But he makes an ongoing case too. Both eulogy and manifesto, Still in a Dream is an enthralling, nostalgic meditation on formative, lost-in-music moments and an eloquent, enduring argument for an art of bliss and bewilderment.

article_text:
Art D’Égypte has announced the final artists participating in its upcoming edition, Forever Is Now .06 , set to take place from 4 to 28 November.

The sixth edition of the event will return to the Giza Pyramids for the first time under the auspices of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, and Experience Egypt and the patronage of UNESCO. Led by Art D’Égypte founder Nadine Abdel Ghaffar, Forever Is Now .06 will recenter the pyramids, bringing the questions of the continuity of creation through time and space to the forefront. It will invite artists to respond, through site-specific installations and new commissions, to these ancient landmarks, repositioning them from historical relic to site of contemporary cultural exchange.

Invited participants in the international and upcoming women-led edition include Egyptian sculptor and painter Reham Abo Elazm, Turkish artist Seçkin Pirim, Jiang Qiong Er from China, British-Jamaican sculptor and performance artist Rochelle-Webster Nembhard, British-French filmmaker Charlotte Colbert, French-American artist Raphaële Shirley, as well as Bernar Venet and Geoffroy Pithon from France.

Forever Is Now .06 runs from 4 to 28 November

To describe the plight of artists who make films and videos, Martine Syms compared the situation to a viral meme starring a giant, vacant head waiting to be filled in with words below a familiar prompt: “Why you so quiet? What’s on your mind?” For her part, Syms said she would fill in that empty noggin with some stark words: “I’m trying to fund my no-budget experimental film.”

There has never been an especially easy time to make moving-image art, which is notoriously hard to monetize. But these days, the challenge is even more formidable because of the abundance of film and video art in the context of biennials, museums, and the art discourse more broadly.

Syms should know. For more than a decade, she has conceived acclaimed videos, installations, and performances about identity, often with a focus on Blackness and meme culture. Such work has earned her representation by three blue-chip galleries, and her 2022 feature film The African Desperate was theatrically distributed by Mubi, the company that would spin the Demi Moore–starring horror movie The Substance into a surprise Oscar contender two years later. She will also be the subject of a Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles survey next year.

But Syms said she still faces a widespread lack of understanding about film/video work and the shortage of funding to accompany it. “I had a collector in Europe ask, ‘Why should I buy video art?’” she told me. “I was like, ‘I don’t fucking know.’” (She later clarified that she hadn’t felt compelled to dignify that collector with an answer, saying, “It has nothing to do with me.”)

The problem is not unique to her, either. When ARTnews surveyed the best artworks of the 21st century so far in 2025, six of the top 10 pieces were moving-image works. One of those was Grosse Fatigue (2013), a widely shown video essay by Camille Henrot about the creation of the universe represented through images and videos clicked open on a computer desktop. Henrot, who debuted her first follow-up moving-image work after more than a decade earlier this year, said that support for such work remains hard to come by, even after endorsements from international institutions and representation by the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth. She recently told Art in America , ARTnews ’s sister publication, “I saw someone commenting about the current art market crisis, suggesting that what sells now is experiences, and also works that are easy to transport. I was like, wait! I have your medium! Film!”

When Syms and I spoke in the spring, I asked why acclaimed video artists like she and Henrot face such trouble. “The big answer, I guess, is that it’s a market imperative,” she said. “Increasingly, there are investors that galleries are reporting to—stakeholder interests. It’s a bigger thing that’s happening across moving images.” She added, “There’s really no way to fund low-budget work.”

Here to help improve the situation, at least in part, is the Vega Foundation , a Toronto-based art organization founded by collector Elisa Nuyten . Vega has supported video artists such as Syms by commissioning new works and showing them in institutions and biennials before adding them to its own collection. For Syms—and other notable artists including Lucy Raven, Jordan Strafer, and Stephanie Comilang—the Vega Foundation has become a lifeline.

Syms is currently at work on a new commission from Vega that will appear in her survey at MOCA LA: RW-LO, which she described as a “film about a Real World superfan in Y2K New Orleans.” (She described the work as being “inspired by a true story,” since the hit MTV reality show’s ninth season was shot in the Big Easy in the year 2000, and added, “I was myself a Real World superfan.”)

Syms said she spent nearly 20 years conceiving the work but it was only recently that the Vega Foundation helped make the project a reality. Having struck up a conversation with the foundation several years ago, she approached Vega with a version of a script. Without much delay, the foundation gave her funding. “They’ve been great to work with,” Syms said. “They’re the best kind of collaborator.”

“I do feel that video art is under-supported,” Nuyten, a new addition to the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list , said in April, speaking from her home in Paris (she splits her time between there and Toronto). She was quick to note that she was surrounded by paintings and sculptures—a landscape by Miriam Cahn and an aquarium by Pierre Huyghe, for example. There were notably few videos, which she conceded can be “hard to live with.” She added: “Collectors often stay away from the medium. That’s why we quickly rose in the art world. Artists like talking to us.”

Founded in 2022, Vega is not the only organization of its kind—there’s also the Fondazione In Between Art Film and the LAS Foundation, both of which were launched in 2019 by collectors (Beatrice Bulgari for the former; Jan Fischer for the latter, working in association with Bettina Kames). But the Vega Foundation stands out as a leader in the field, with commissions regularly popping up in biennials and museums. Often, the only way to know about the foundation’s involvement in a project is to read the fine print on a wall text. Still, Vega’s behind-the-scenes efforts have helped to shape video art as it stands today.

One of the foundation’s first commissions was for Ali Cherri, a Lebanese artist whose Vega-supported film The Dam (2022) centers on a Sundanese bricklayer who, in his spare time, begins making a mud creation near the Nile. The film showed in the 2022 Venice Biennale, where it won the Silver Lion for an emerging artist; the jury praised Cherri’s work for its ability to bring “a meditation on earth, fire and water from a constructive perspective to a mythical dimension.” That same year, a version of it was screened at the Cannes Film Festival.

More recently, Vega helped fund Diego Marcon’s Krapfen (2025), a film in which a child is taunted by invisible beings that sing and dance. (Marcon, a young Italian artist with a flair for eerie, exquisite absurdism , rendered those beings as see-through by using green-screen technology.) Krapfen made its debut in 2025 at the Renaissance Society in Chicago, where Newcity praised it as a “must-see,” and then formed the centerpiece of a Marcon solo show that opened this past summer at the Art Gallery of Ontario and is now on view at New York’s New Museum, where Nuyten is a trustee.

Between the Cherri and Marcon works, Vega commissioned artists such as Sharon Lockhart, an American filmmaker who used the foundation’s funding to shoot on Fogo Island, off the coast of Newfoundland; Alia Farid, a Kuwaiti biennial-circuit staple whose Vega project took her to southern Iraq; and Aria Dean, a rising American star whose widely praised video Abattoir, U.S.A.! (2023) centers on a slaughterhouse that she rendered digitally; and Lap-See Lam, a Swedish phenom whose films have pondered aspects of the Chinese diaspora. Vega’s adventurous support continued this year by acting as a co-producer on a Fondazione In Between Art Film commission by Yuyan Wang, who unveiled a film about robots and animatronics as part of a show in Venice.

Julia Paoli, the Vega Foundation’s curator, said she decides which projects to fund based in part on studio visits with artists. “We’re really trying to understand what artists are thinking through and working on, and also what our colleagues and peers are thinking about, so that we can stay rigorous,” she said. She also considers whether an artist or their work bears any connection to Canada, or whether a potential video commission could be presented with a partner institution there.

Otherwise, Paoli noted few parameters for a Vega commission, saying that each budget is tailor-made to its recipient. The budgets also come with a plan for where to present the work, be it a biennial, a film festival, or a museum. “We’re talking about the production of incredibly rigorous, complicated work, so I’m coming at it from a deeply researched curatorial perspective,” Paoli said of such expensive and time-consuming projects. “These are high-stakes.”

The Vega Foundation grew out of Nuyten’s collecting. Raised in Belgium, she started Vitamine Chic, a wholesale fashion agency in Toronto that she ran from 1988 until she sold it in 1998. Around 20 years ago, while traveling in Europe, Nuyten began buying art. “I decided I wanted to apply myself to contemporary art and learn about it,” she said. “I didn’t have an art history degree, but I went to local galleries. Slowly, I started to travel more and to collect more. I wanted art on my walls—I wanted interesting things for my children, and for us as a family, to respond to.”

Nuyten’s collection now includes quite a bit of historical art, by artists ranging from the Surrealist painter Leonor Fini to the French sculptor Louise Bourgeois, as well as works by some of today’s most famous living artists: Sarah Lucas, Philippe Parreno, Luc Tuymans, and others. But Nuyten spoke most highly of the “younger generations of artists” working today, many of whom are attracted to video. Starting the Vega Foundation was an attempt to connect with such stars in the making. “It was a very easy decision,” Nuyten said. “I felt that it would allow me to stay relevant” and reach “more experimental, more political voices.”

She was specific about the political aspect of what she does, recalling that amid Israel’s war in Gaza she told her colleagues at Vega Foundation, “Let’s support the film of a great Palestinian artist.” With Palestinian artists facing pushback, and in some cases censorship, in mainstream institutions, Vega threw its support behind the Berlin-based filmmaker Basma Al-Sharif, whose 2025 commission Morning Circle focuses on an Armenian man and his Jordanian son in Germany. Though the film doesn’t directly address the war in Gaza, it was politicized in Germany. When al-Sharif screened it at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf this year, Jewish organizations and conservative politicians issued public denouncements of both the artist and the storied art school, in what the artist Adam Broomberg and writer Michele Faguet described as a “smear campaign” in a Hyperallergic defense of al-Sharif’s film . In mind of supporting work of the kind, Nuyten said, “We want to help. We can be more political with our organization.”

The Vega Foundation is currently gearing up for its fifth year, and Nuyten has been thinking about its future. “I don’t want to become the LUMA Foundation,” she said, referring to collector Maja Hoffmann’s long-running art organization that went on to open a Frank Gehry–designed museum in Arles, France. “I don’t want to open a space.”

Asked why not, she scrunched up her face. “To have a permanent space, that almost makes me feel a bit claustrophobic. It would be so non-dynamic—the opposite of what we want to be.”

A version of this article that appeared in print stated that Basma Al-Sharif’s film focused on Palestinian woman. In fact, it centers on an Armenian father and his Jordanian son.

9のプロジェクトを、国際的なコミッティが選出

次世代のクリエイターが異業種でチームを組み、プロダクトデザインの新しい価値を探るデザインイベント 「alter. 2026, Tokyo」 が、10月29日から11月1日までの4日間、 日本橋三井ホール で開催される。

alter.（アルター）は、プロトタイピングとコラボレーションを通じてプロダクトデザインの価値を更新することを目指すプロジェクト。2年目となる今年は、グローバルなデザインシーンを牽引するコミッティメンバーによる審査を経て選出されたプロジェクトを中心に、国内外から75名のクリエイターが参加する。出展者はプロダクトデザイナーにとどまらず、アーティスト、建築家、写真家、職人、エンジニア、研究者など幅広い。

審査を担うのは、建築、プロダクト、ファッション、キュレーション、編集、ジャーナリズムを横断する5名のコミッティメンバーだ。パリを拠点とするアーティスティック・ディレクターの ダン・ソーリー 、英国のデザイナーの フェイ・トゥーグッド 、ヴィトラ・デザイン・ミュージアムのキュレーターの ヨハン・デュレル 、建築家で京都市京セラ美術館館長の 青木淳 、ミラノを拠点とするジャーナリストの ローラ・メイ・トッド が名を連ねる。

見本市型の一般的な形式とは異なり、出展料は無料で、規模に応じて最大300万円の制作補助が支給される点も特徴だ。個別のブースを並べるのではなく、プロダクトと展示空間、来場者の体験を一体のインスタレーションとして評価し、会場全体をひとつの展覧会として構成する。

展示作品の購入やトーク収録も

今年は、プロジェクト展示の「EXHIBITION」に加え、新たに複数のプログラムが設けられる。そのひとつ「CIRCUIT」は、「回路」と「循環」を意味する新プログラムで、プロトタイプを展示で終わらせず、社会や暮らしに届ける道すじを作る。2026年の採択作品のほか、2025年のプロトタイプの現在形、企業とアーティストによる実験的な制作物、alter.がキュレーションした商品を紹介・販売し、会場の展示作品も購入できる。

また「LOUNGE」は、展示される家具やオブジェクトの一部に実際に座り、触れて、過ごせる今年新設の場だ。併設の「STUDIO」では、出展者やゲストによるトークを公開収録し、会期中から会期後にかけてオンラインで発信する。

さらに「AWARD」では、全プロジェクトがコミッティに向けてプレゼンテーションを行い、各メンバーが自らの価値基準で最優秀プロジェクトを選出する。結果は会期の後半に発表される。制作の過程やコミッティによる批評は、日英バイリンガルのアーカイヴブックと、公式ウェブサイト内の「JOURNAL」でも記録・発信される。

参加クリエイターには、市森天颯、菊田潤、柳澤春馬、Sisan Lee、浅野純平、高田一正（PAN-PROJECTS）、大道くらら、松田将英、荒井優作、小林椋、有本怜生、今井悠喜ら、国内外の若手が名を連ねる。

I n terms of attention-demanding loglines, this year’s Sundance has a few. There’s the body horror Saccharine, about a diet craze that involves eating human ashes, midnight movie Buddy , about a Barney-esque kids TV star who starts murdering children and then there’s Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant which, well, you can probably imagine.

But the annual “wait, what?” prize easily goes to the offbeat fable Wicker, the story of a smelly spinster fisherwoman who commissions herself a husband made of, that’s right, wicker. While the film does have its expected amount of audience-provoking moments – wicker-fucking bringing the most noise both on and off the screen – to its credit, there’s an attempt to give us more than just easy shock value, something that can’t always be said for films in this often tedious category. Writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, who previously brought the mostly likable alien invasion comedy Save Yourselves! to the festival, use their far-out premise to touch upon more of-our-world issues like the patriarchal cruelty of marriage and the special fury reserved for those who dare to live outside of the accepted rules. They succeed in brief flashes but ultimately, there’s too much here that doesn’t gel, a tonally uneven mix of mostly unfunny bawdy humour, dark fantasy and unlikely romance, too much wood but not enough fire.

Olivia Colman, who has had mixed results at Sundance ranging from The Father to Jimpa, is Fisherwoman, whose smell is as remarked upon as her singledom. She’s largely immune to the insults, though, happily removed from the archaic gender roles that curse the local village. But after she sneers through another comically awful wedding, the jabs start to have an effect and rather than laughing it away, she asks the local basket-maker (Peter Dinklage, forever seeming like he’s on the verge of breaking into song) to make her a husband. A month later, he arrives.

There’s admirable ambition to the film-making, an intricately built world that meshes mostly old with bits of the new. Like many a fairytale, it’s a society built around the importance of men and the deference of women. Men are known by their profession and women by their relationship to their husband. The wedding ritual sees the man not offer his wife a ring but insist a collar upon her. Fisherwoman’s flagrant refusal to play by the rules, to take charge of her own life as breadwinner, throws the community into disarray. The women, led by Elizabeth Debicki’s spiralling queen bee, are both horrified and perhaps a little jealous, maybe even aroused by her new husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård in impressively handsome wicker (the effects work here is top notch). The men are worried about what his sexual and domestic perfection means for them and how their wives see them. Can anyone be happy any more?

The central relationship is taken seriously enough for us to want more than we’re ultimately given. His arrival asks so many questions – what does he know, what does he want, what does she need, what was she missing – yet their early scenes are mostly based around comically vigorous sex (questions about splinters are also never answered) rather than any real development. He’s a commission designed to love her but there’s no exploration of what this means for their relationship and any agency he might want or need. These might sound like silly thoughts to have while watching a film like this but we’re meant to be emotionally invested in what happens. When conflict comes it’s mostly simple and soapy – has he shagged anyone else in town – and while there’s an effective scene of Colman breaking down while explaining the difficulties of sharing a life that had previously been lived alone (she remains one of our great criers) it’s too little too late. We don’t know anything of his reaction to the world or who he really is, just his blind devotion to her and when tragedy inevitably strikes, there’s just no real attachment to any of it. I was thinking about how invested I was in the admittedly more dramatic but even less verbal relationship between Sally Hawkins and the fish man in The Shape of Water. There are ways to make us care in fantastically odd romances such as this, I just don’t think Fischer and Wilson were able to find them.

It’s hard to imagine many other working actors taking on the fisherwoman role, Colman often seeming like the rare actor whose career has allowed certain films to exist. I haven’t loved her choices of late (The Roses, Jimpa, Wicked Little Letters) but she’s never less then entirely devoted to often far-out bits and she gives this her all even though I wish the script afforded her more depth. She knows how to oscillate between broad comedy and heart-wrenching drama but the film around her isn’t as adept. Like the dream husband at its centre, Wicker looks the part but there’s nothing underneath.

article_text:
As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside the likes of La Binoche and La Deneuve — it’s immediately, amusingly jarring to see Isabelle Huppert cast as a thoroughly indefinite article: a jobbing movie extra whose name nobody recalls, no matter how many headshots and résumés she desperately forces into the hands of higher-ups on set. Casting Huppert as an industry nobody is the chief gag of “ All About Corinne ,” Marc Fitoussi ‘s winningly droll film-biz comedy, but there turns out to be a lot of mileage in it, particularly with co-star Sandrine Kiberlain — cast not just as an industry somebody, but as Sandrine Kiberlain herself — as her imperious foil.

Both sending themselves up in contrasting ways, the stars’ perceptive, vanity-free performances lend some weight and feeling to what is otherwise a frothy exercise — as is to be expected from Fitoussi, a specialist in female-driven French divertissements , including the uncharacteristically chipper Huppert vehicle “Copacabana” and the recent Laure Calamy hit “Two Tickets to Greece.” Given its starry, easy-breezy charms and accessibly inside-baseball humor, “All About Corinne” should have little trouble securing global arthouse distribution following a festival run that began as Locarno’s closing night selection, continuing through gala slots in Toronto and Busan; audiences au fait with “Call Your Agent!” and its good-humored brand of industry satire will feel right at home.

“You might want to ask yourself why you’re still in the same place at your age,” says a colleague, with casual cruelty, to Corinne Maclou (Huppert), an actress who, for decades, has been steadily and invisibly working at the least glamorous end of the business — and who, in her sixties, hasn’t yet given up hope of stardom. In fringe theater, at least, she’s had the odd inspired moment in the spotlight; in film, she’s lumped with countless other, younger extras and bit players, fighting for the rare gift of a single line.

Not for lack of ability — Huppert may dim her light a bit, but doesn’t stretch so far as to play a bad actor — she’s simply never had the break, and while Corinne’s efforts to ingratiate herself with A-listers are played for squirm-inducing comedy, there’s also gentle pathos to her desperation, underlined by the ironic star casting. She knows, and we know, that she’s a Huppert-level talent. Why can no one else see it?

Corinne’s standard line to try curry favor with bigger-name actresses is to cheerfully remark on their physical resemblance to each other, noting that they could play sisters — an approach that doesn’t get the diminutive redhead far with the tall, beachy-haired Kiberlain when they share a scene (or at least occupy the same frame) together. But Corinne’s persistence coincides with a sudden phase of insecurity for the soignée leading lady, who’s trying to cultivate a more down-to-earth image after her agent pithily tells her that “even Cotillard is less detached from reality.” And so she pityingly takes Corinne’s CV, as well as the proferred recording of an obscure Chilean play which Corinne believes to be her finest hour.

Nothing comes of it, of course, until months later, when Corinne sees the news that Kiberlain is taking to the Paris stage in a production of the very same play, and bitterly confronts her outside the theater. Out of resentment and shamefaced guilt, a highly conditional friendship is forged, as each actress uses the other to very different ends: In Kiberlain, Corinne sees her long-awaited connection to the top; through Corinne, Kiberlain believes she can keep it real. Fitoussi’s writing is fizzy and lightly bitchy throughout, but it’s the stars, playing freely with their respective screen personae, who make it genuinely funny. In a more obvious iteration of this story, their roles might be swapped: There’s as much inherent comedy in Huppert playing a spiraling, faintly tragic rube as in Kiberlain, best known for her neurotic comic work, revealing the brittle hauteur of her “real” self.

Other good sports turning up as themselves, to wickedly unflattering effect, include Emmanuelle Bercot, tetchily directing a big-budget period drama that could turn things around for Corinne, and Diane Kruger — hilariously glamazonian as she competes with Kiberlain for maximum miscasting in a new Dardenne Brothers film about a tiler in Liège. If that raises a chuckle from you, as it certainly did from this critic, then consider yourself squarely in the film’s target audience. You can cut precisely without cutting too deep: More sweet than scathing, “All About Corinne” loves its stars too much to really draw blood. We love them too, so that’s just fine.

article_text:
H ere is an engaging family movie from the Portland-based Laika studio that created Coraline . It is a fantasy adventure in Laika’s distinctively crafted stop-motion animation, written by Chris Butler from the bestseller of the same title by Carson Ellis and Colin Meloy, the latter being a band member of The Decemberists , one of whose tour posters we duly glimpse in this film. The director is Laika’s lead animator Travis Knight. It’s a forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale which CS Lewis and JRR Tolkien might have recognised, a story about the mysterious glory of going on a quest and the terrible fear and wish-fulfilment euphoria of being called upon to confront secret forces that the grownups know nothing about.

The setting is modern-day Portland , Oregon, a groovy city whose hipster-ish stores (there’s a coffee shop actually called Dripster) and Woke 1.0 signage are affectionately mocked. But most of all, the film is aware of a huge forest park next to the city, a place here mythologised as the impassable wilderness or “wildwood” where strange creatures, fairytale nobility and wisecracking talking animals reputedly dwell, of which the city-dwelling humans are entirely ignorant. Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is a 12-year-old girl whose parents (voiced by Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) are a couple of amiable hippies who believe in natural forces and benign magic. They have another child, Prue’s baby brother Mac, who Prue has to look after one day, pushing him in his stroller around the city and having to endure a certain classmate of hers tagging along. This is nerdy Curtis (Jacob Tremblay) who has a crush on her.

They are stunned when a bunch (or rather a murder) of crows gather with Hitchcockian menace in a kids’ play area, swoop down and carry poor little Mac off to their forest domain. Plucky (and also terrified) Prue and Curtis give chase and enter the dark and trackless forest, and find it is a parallel world, undreamt of by the ordinary human world, populated by all manner of loquacious beasts and oppressed humans. Their rule is divided between the supercilious and incompetent governor (Marc Evan Jackson) and the evil dowager governess, voiced with relish by Carey Mulligan , who has at her command a redcoat army of coyotes.

The dowager governess has a wrenching sadness in her heart, due to an awful loss and a tragic attempt at a cover-up, which the film shows us in the opening section. Prue and Curtis, though separated by the action, are to come together for their big showdown with this wicked witch of the forest and a reckoning also with the Wildwood’s bandit leader and freedom fighter Brendan, voiced by Mahershala Ali .

The stop-motion animation style has, as with Coraline, a robust and pleasing directness, and results in, for me, a more organic character and physical immediacy than Pixar’s ubiquitous digital look, to which it makes a welcome change. I wasn’t sure that the narrative delivered a satisfyingly clear motive for the governess’s reprehensible plan, and in fact the story itself did not have the scary punch of Coraline, except in the uncanny opening sequence. Then again, it’s not that kind of story.

A news item by ArtThrob Editors on the 22nd of September 2026. This should take you 2 minutes to read.

From November 26, 2026, to February 28, 2027, the Bienal de Yucatán will launch the first international contemporary art festival in Mexico. The first edition of the Bienal will bring together 76 national and international artists across four exhibitions within a circuit of 16 venues throughout the historic center of Mérida and the municipality of Maní, with free admission for all. The Bienal de Yucatán is a long-term project with three initial editions scheduled to take place in 2026, 2028, and 2030.

The first edition, titled VOCAL , is dedicated to a reflection on tongue, languages, and multiple forms of communication. The central exhibition of the same name, under the artistic direction of artist Abraham Cruzvillegas, will present 38 new commissions, 42 Mexican artists – including 18 from the region – and 34 international artists from 20 countries. The Bienal de Yucatán will offer a space for critical thinking, artistic experimentation, and contemporary cultural dialogue from the Mexican Southeast.

Yucatán: Cultural Territory Mérida offers an exceptional context as a territory where the richness of living Maya culture, tangible historical heritage, and a community with growing cultural infrastructure coexist – comprising museums, cultural centers, self-managed spaces, artist studios, forums, and universities, including the National University of the Arts of Yucatán (UNAY).

The name “Yucatán,” according to one of the most widespread interpretations, derives from a linguistic misunderstanding between Maya peoples and Spanish conquistadors: a first encounter marked by the complexity of translation. The Bienal takes up that narrative as a starting point to propose a space dedicated to building common languages – in the plural.

The Bienal de Yucatán is born from the conviction that Mérida and the Mexican Southeast harbor an extraordinary artistic energy that deserves an international platform to match. This is a project growing out of the territory, with the ambition of positioning Yucatán as a hub for critical and creative thought, in dialogue with the Caribbean and the world.

VOCAL VOCAL, under the artistic direction of artist Abraham Cruzvillegas, offers a reflection on tongue, languages, idioms, the written, the spoken, and what needs to be said. The showcase unfolds at the main venue, Casa de la Cultura del Mayab (a former 16th-century convent under SEDECULTA), and extends across different venues in Mérida’s historic center and the municipality of Maní.

Mayan culture developed an elaborate system of representing oral language, manifested in documents carved in stone that resisted destruction and looting since the colonial period. It has been the people who still speak Maya who have sustained the survival of their language, despite the efforts of a monolithic national will that attempted to erase cultural and linguistic diversity.

VOCAL brings together 76 artists and other participants–including linguists, filmmakers, poets, musicians, and dancers–who, as Cruzvillegas points out, offer us “words that affirm difference together, and that would together imagine other possible landscapes, and other ways of existing within them, collectively.”

“This international exhibition will focus primarily on tongue, languages, idioms, the written, the spoken, and what needs to be said. The works and individuals participating in this renewed version of the Bienal de Yucatán will make it one of inclusion and diversity, of languages and idioms that engage in dialogue and contradict one another.”

– Abraham Cruzvillegas , Artistic Director of the Bienal de Yucatán 2026
